In its four Old Testament occurrences, it is rendered “comfort” and “recover,” showing that the word can describe either giving consolation or regaining well-being, depending on the sentence. Its use is found in Job, Psalms, and Amos, where the surrounding wording determines how this movement toward relief is understood.

It appears 44 times in the Old Testament, often in descriptions of the abundance and goodness of the land God promised to Israel. The word can also occur as something given, brought, or enjoyed, but its basic meaning remains milk. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

“Fury” describes intense, uncontrolled anger. This Hebrew word appears only twice in the Old Testament corpus, both times in Daniel 3, and both English renderings are “fury.” It functions as a noun naming a powerful emotional response rather than an action or person. The word’s basic sense is therefore a state of fierce anger. Its precise force in either occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: “Possession” is the central meaning of this Hebrew word. It names something held by a person or group, often an allotted holding such as land. The word functions as a term for what is received, retained, or assigned as belonging to someone. It occurs 66 times in the Old Testament, with repeated connections to giving and assigning such holdings. Its normal sense is therefore a possession understood as something granted or held as one's own.

This Hebrew word is a proper name rendered “Heshmon,” rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 15:27. Because the available context does not include the verse text or a lexical definition, its precise identity must be taken from that passage; the word itself is preserved as the name Heshmon in English renderings.

The word means “decree.” It refers to a formal decision or order issued by recognized authority, especially in settings involving kings and governments. Its use can identify the decree itself or describe an action established by such a decree. This Hebrew Old Testament word occurs 24 times, with most occurrences in Ezra and the remainder in Daniel, where official decisions and royal authority are prominent. It therefore carries the sense of an authoritative ruling within an administrative or royal setting.

Its precise force in Psalm 55:22 depends on the surrounding verse text, but the central idea is a burden that can be transferred to another party.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a branch of a plant, rendered “branch” or “branches.” It functions as a noun naming a part that grows out from a tree or other plant. The word occurs six times in the Old Testament, in Job, Psalms, Ezekiel, and Hosea, where branch language contributes to descriptions of plant growth and imagery. Its ordinary sense remains focused on a branch rather than on the whole tree or plant.

Jotbah is a Hebrew place-name, referring to a location rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Kings 21:19, and the English renderings preserve it as “Jotbah.” Because it functions as a proper name, its lexical role is to identify that place; the surrounding verse is needed to explain its significance there.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “brightness.” It refers to visible brightness or shining appearance as a noun-like description of what is seen. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Ezekiel 28:7 and 28:17. Its use identifies brightness as something associated with the person or object being described, while the surrounding verse determines its precise force in each occurrence.

This Hebrew word means “lies.” It functions as a naming word for falsehood—what is spoken or practiced falsely—rather than describing a person or place. It occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with five of those occurrences rendered “lies.” Its uses appear in Job, Psalms, Hosea, and Nahum, showing a consistent reference to falsehood across different passages. In Hosea 10:13, it is connected with actions and their resulting consequences, helping present lies as something people produce or rely upon.

Coniah is a personal name, referring to the individual identified by that name in Jeremiah. It is rendered “Coniah” in all three recorded Hebrew occurrences, so its role is to identify a person rather than express an action, quality, or idea. The name appears in Jeremiah 22:24, Jeremiah 22:28, and Jeremiah 37:1. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Hebrew word describes the action of being “bowed,” referring to a posture in which a person or something is brought downward. It functions as a verb, expressing the act or condition of bending low. The word occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing three times in Psalms and once each in Isaiah and Micah. Its use can describe physical lowering, while the surrounding verse determines the particular situation.

This Hebrew word means “feed,” describing the act of providing food. It functions as a verb, expressing an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at Genesis 25:30, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated occurrences. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but the basic idea is giving food.

This Hebrew noun refers to a “mortar,” the vessel or basin used for pounding and grinding food or other materials. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Numbers 11:8, and its rendering there points to this practical household object. The word names the tool itself rather than the action of crushing or the material being prepared. Its exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew noun means “marrow,” the substance found within bones. It names an inner bodily substance rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Job 21:24, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but the word itself refers plainly to marrow as something associated with the interior of the bones.

This Hebrew noun means “perfection.” It identifies the quality or condition of being perfect rather than describing an action. It functions as a noun for what is characterized by perfection. In the Hebrew Bible, it occurs once, in Psalm 50:2, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage, but the central idea remains perfection.

This Hebrew verb means “reigned.” It tells what a king or ruler did, or identifies the period in which that person held kingship. The word is used 351 times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, showing its regular use in accounts of kings and their years of leadership. It can describe the beginning, duration, or succession of a king’s reign. Its normal emphasis is on exercising royal authority rather than merely being called a king.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise ordinary meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Bible, at Judges 6:2. The available record identifies the Hebrew word and its single occurrence, but provides no explicit definition, approved meaning term, or English rendering. Therefore, its meaning should be understood from the full verse and surrounding passage rather than from this word entry alone.

It occurs 14 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in passages connected with both personal loss and national calamity. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word describes something as “burdensome,” functioning as a descriptive term rather than naming a person or action. It presents the thing in view as difficult to bear or carry in the sentence. It occurs once in the Old Testament, in Zechariah 12:3, so its precise force there belongs to that verse’s surrounding context. Its normal sense remains clear even though the verse text is not included here.

This Hebrew word describes something as “supple,” presenting it as having a flexible or yielding quality. It functions as a descriptive term rather than naming a person, place, or action. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 16:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its basic lexical sense is the quality expressed by “supple.”

The word occurs 304 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it describes a broad and recurring way Scripture speaks about family relationships and communities.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “oxen,” functioning as a noun for these animals. It occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in passages that mention them among livestock or animals under consideration. The word is found in Deuteronomy, Judges, Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah, so its basic reference remains consistent across several kinds of passages. Its exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word refers to brass, a hard metal or metallic material. It is used as a noun for something valued for strength and durability, including metal associated with weapons, tools, or other solid objects. The word occurs ten times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with its uses spread across several books. Its normal sense remains a durable metal substance; the surrounding verse determines the particular object or comparison being described.

Naarai is a personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 11:37, and is rendered “Naarai.” Because the available information gives no separate definition or description, the word should be understood primarily as the person’s name. Its exact significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s place in the account.

This Hebrew word describes someone as “unpunished” or “be,” especially in the sense of being clear from guilt or penalty. It can describe a person who is not held guilty, or state that someone will not escape accountability. The word occurs 44 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages concerning false use of God’s name, personal innocence, and the consequences of wrongdoing. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “weapons”—equipment used for fighting or warfare. It functions as a noun for such battle gear, appearing in descriptions of people receiving, carrying, or being equipped with it. The word occurs 10 times in the Old Testament corpus, including passages involving kings, soldiers, and a warlike horse. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “thick.” It functions as an adjective, describing something by its physical thickness or substantial form. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing once each in Deuteronomy, 1 Kings, and 2 Chronicles. Its clearest recorded English rendering is “thick,” while the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and subject.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “chains.” It names a connected object and can function as something made, given, or used to restrain. In the Old Testament, it occurs 24 times across 23 verses, including descriptions connected with priestly garments and an instance involving Samson’s restraint. Its central idea remains a chain: something formed of linked parts for adornment, attachment, or restraint. The exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “pressed,” describing a condition in which something is forced down or heavily burdened. It functions as an action or condition rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Amos 2:13, so its usage is concentrated rather than widespread. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Hebrew word means “signet.” It names a tangible object rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament data, it occurs twice, with both occurrences in Daniel 6:17. That concentrated use identifies its ordinary lexical sense, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific details of how the signet functions there. The word is therefore best understood simply as a signet, without extending its meaning beyond that established sense.

This Hebrew word means “Most” and describes the highest rank or position. In Daniel, it is used in expressions referring to the Most High, presenting God as above all earthly rulers and powers. The word occurs 18 times in the Hebrew Bible, all within Daniel, so its normal scriptural use is closely associated with language about God’s supreme standing. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

Azmon is a place-name, referring to a location on Israel’s southern boundary. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a stated definition; it functions as the proper name of a geographic site. The Hebrew word occurs three times in the Old Testament corpus, in two boundary descriptions in Numbers and one in Joshua. In each supplied rendering, it appears as “Azmon,” confirming that the name is carried over rather than translated into an English meaning. Its precise location and significance must therefore be understood from the surrounding boundary passages.

Pedahel is a personal name, referring to one particular individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In English Bible renderings, it appears as “Pedahel.” This Hebrew name occurs once in the Old Testament, at Numbers 34:28. Because it functions as a name, its basic role is to identify the person being mentioned; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific role in the passage.

This Hebrew word means “smite.” It is a verb, so it names an action rather than a person, place, or object. The word appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Nahum 2:10, and is rendered “smite” there. Because it occurs only once and no verse text is provided here, its precise role in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic lexical force remains the action expressed by “smite,” without adding other meanings from translation wording.

This Hebrew verb means to tear or rend something, especially by pulling it apart. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. e.t: Sarah is a personal name, referring to the woman known as Abraham’s wife and Isaac’s mother. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it is used as a proper name rather than as a general description or action. The name appears 38 times in the Hebrew corpus, almost entirely in Genesis, where it is connected with Abraham’s household, the promised birth of Isaac, and Sarah’s place in the family’s history. It also appears once in Isaiah’s remembrance of Abraham and Sarah. Its approved English rendering is “Sarah.”
